These devices bring enough voltage and amperage to bring a dead battery back to life. They can also fill a low tire or pump up a leaky one until the driver can make it to a service station for repairs. Ahead, learn the most important factors to consider when choosing one of these combo units and find out how the following models earned a spot on our lineup of the best jump starters with air compressors.

Bottom line: Jump starters with air compressors are essential tools for emergencies, offering reliable performance and versatility. DeWalt leads the pack with its superior features.

There might be a lot to know about these versatile devices, but shopping for the best jump starter with an air compressor doesn’t have to be complicated. The DeWalt jump starter/compressor combo performed flawlessly in our hands-on tests, easily earning the title of the best overall model. This unit supplies enough juice to start depleted batteries and has a built-in alternator tester.

We got an alternator reading by connecting it to a vehicle’s battery terminals when the vehicle was idling. Since problems starting a vehicle can be due to a faulty alternator, this feature is a nice perk.

The clamps are large and grip the terminals firmly. We were able to get a reading of the current battery voltage. When we connected the terminals to a fully charged battery, the DeWalt indicated the voltage, which is a good way to see the battery’s current charge.

The compressor measured the existing pressure in the tires. We were able to preselect the amount of air we wanted to add, and the compressor inflated the tires to the exact pressure. This handy feature removes the guesswork, especially when inflating bicycle tires that can explode if too much pressure is applied. What our tester says: “The DeWalt jump starter was a dream to use—its multifunctionality and high-quality performance made jumping batteries and filling tires almost effortless.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DeWalt jump starter with air compressor at Tractor Supply Co., Amazon, or The Home Depot.

Jump starters with air compressors can be incredibly versatile, and this model from DieHard definitely fits the bill. The lead-acid jump starter offers 950 peak amps for cranking over large diesel engines as well as reverse hookup protection to avoid damaging the expensive electrical components that are sometimes vulnerable during jumping. It also features two 12V ports and a USB port for charging devices.

The compressor produces up to 150 PSI of pressure and includes a digital gauge for presetting the pressure and checking the battery’s charge level. The Trekure jump starter fits a lot of energy into a small package, making it a good option for taking along on road trips. We didn’t have any problems jump-starting three different dead batteries, but the clamps are a little on the small side—we would have appreciated larger clamps.

This unit came with some battery charge, but once it was depleted by testing, it took about 6 hours to recharge. We liked its bright LED flashlight, which allowed us to see what we were doing after dark. The flashlight also doubles as a yellow flashing road flare that can be seen from a distance.

It also features a 150 PSI air compressor with an analog gauge for pumping flat tires and a high-volume air port for filling air mattresses and pool floats.

The Schumacher features two 12-volt (V) charging ports, two standard 120V outlets, and a USB port for charging mobile devices. This allows it to charge several devices or act as an emergency power station if the power goes out in the home. Its cables wrap around the unit and clip onto the base for storage, and the compressor hose stores in a small compartment in the back.

We weren’t big fans of the tire pressure gauge, which was not lit and wasn’t very accurate (a difference of around 8 PSI), and it’s in a weird spot (on the back of the jump pack and obscured by the clamp). But otherwise, the unit had plenty of power to jump the car and it was easy to use. We liked the 120V outlets.

For an additional well-rounded jump starter, Stanley’s J5C09 portable power station could fit the bill. This jump starter features a lead-acid battery with up to 10,000A of cranking power for turning over large engines in gasoline and diesel vehicles alike. It also includes a 120 PSI compressor that can fill nearly any tire, with an illuminated analog gauge for monitoring the pressure in real-time.

This unit provides some additional built-in features worth noting. It offers a USB port for charging devices, a standard 12V port, a reverse polarity alarm to indicate improperly installed clamps, and a positionable work light for shedding light on the repair area.

During the test, the one feature that stood out the most was the air compressor. It was able to fill a tire in much less time than the other models (about 4 minutes), and the analog display was very accurate. It’s also easy to set up and use in the dark, plus it features extra-long cables to make reaching battery terminals easier. It also had plenty of power to kick the vehicle’s engine over. The positionable light is a nice touch as it allowed us to position the jump pack carefully without losing our light source. The light is a bit weak, however.

If you’re looking for a multi-function jump starter/compressor combo, check out this new model from JackPak. Right out of the box, we were impressed with this unit’s build quality—it’s solid, rugged, and comes with heavy-duty clamps.

Like the DeWalt that earned our best overall award, the JackPak shows how many volts the current vehicle battery has, which is great if there isn’t a voltmeter handy. We wish all the units came with this feature.

We liked the bright LED light on the JackPak, and it doubles as a powerbank for charging devices. It also features a low-power sleep mode that keeps its internal battery from discharging for up to 36 months.

Get the JackPack jump starter with air compressor at Lowe’s or The Home Depot.

When a battery goes dead and a car is stuck in a parking lot or across town (or the side of the road), there’s a lot on the line. We know that, so we tested the jump starters with air compressors on our own depleted car and truck batteries and to inflate a range of tires.

We tested each product by jumping a dead car, truck, and riding mower batteries. We also used a multimeter to determine the voltage from the jump starters. We tested the jump starters over a 2-week period, connecting each one to the various battery terminals and then attempting to start the vehicle.

We also drained some of the air from bike, car, and truck tires to test the built-in compressors. For the inflation tests, we partially deflated bike, car, and truck tires and then timed how long it took each inflator to return the tires to the recommended pressure. During these inflation tests, we paid close attention to how easily the air chucks connected to the valve stems, whether they created a secure seal, and how well they held up through repeated use. We also considered whether the compressors operated consistently under pressure or showed signs of strain, as well as how intuitive and responsive the controls were throughout the process.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a jump starter/inflator did on a test or assessment, the higher the points. The products that excelled were given awards based on their strengths, while those that failed were removed from our lineup.

Carrying a jump starter with an air compressor means drivers can handle emergencies and repairs without calling for help (or when help isn’t available). And who doesn’t enjoy a little self-reliance? These devices include built-in jumper cables to clamp onto the positive and negative terminals of a dead battery. It sounds straightforward, but shopping for one of these devices requires a bit of background and know-how. The following sections will break down the most important considerations to keep in mind while shopping for a battery jumper with air compressor.

Jump starters equipped with air compressors include one of two battery types: lithium-ion and lead-acid.

The best jump starters with air compressors—and all portable jump starters, for that matter—have an onboard battery that provides ample power to start a vehicle or operate the compressor. In most cases, the battery size of these portable chargers is described in milliampere hours (mAh) or amp hours (Ah)—1,000mAh equals 1Ah.

Higher mAh or Ah ratings equals a larger capacity to store power, so higher ratings mean more batteries charged and tires inflated between recharges. Generally speaking, most portable jump starters use batteries between 10,000 and 35,000mAh. Remember that higher capacity batteries are heavy, and get heavier as the storage increases.

The purpose of a jump starter is to provide a vehicle with enough power to turn over and fire up the engine, then allow the vehicle’s alternator to continue charging the battery. The amount of power a jump starter needs to accomplish this task is determined by the engine.

Small gasoline engines, such as four-cylinder engines found in most cars (and progressively larger vehicles) don’t require much power. But larger eight-cylinder engines require a bit more. And, because of the extremely high compression ratios of diesel engines, large models found in heavy-duty pickups, RVs, and power equipment require even more power. In general, 1,000A or more will do the trick.

Many manufacturers today don’t explicitly list the amount of power provided by their chargers. Instead, they discuss the types of engines their chargers can handle. This is only a concern for diesel vehicles, as any jump starter will handle most gasoline engines.

While it might seem that jumper cables are all created equal, modern jump starters offer additional safety features. Today’s models protect a vehicle’s electrical system and the person using the cables from sparking or reverse polarity, which happens when the user connects the clamps to the wrong terminals—something that’s very easy to do in the dark. Reverse polarity can wreak havoc on the sensitive electronics in today’s vehicles, so this is a crucial feature.

These units will detect the reverse polarity or contact between the clamps and prevent the unit from expelling stored energy through them. Often, a small light or audible alarm will alert the user so you can understand what’s occurring and why the jump starter isn’t charging the vehicle.

When choosing the best jump starter with an air compressor, there is some variance in the amount of pounds per square inch (PSI) offered by these models. Most models produce around 100 PSI—more than enough for any road vehicle’s tires. Most vehicle tires require just 30 to 40 PSI.

Some models offer 150 PSI or more, which is as much pressure as a traditional home air compressor. Are they necessary for typical vehicle repairs? No. But it might take these compressors less time to boost up a tire on the side of the road, so they could be worth the consideration and splurge.

Several additional features might make a portable jump starter with an air compressor a bit more attractive to consumers.

Even with all of this background on choosing the best jump starter with air compressor, you might have questions. The following section is a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about battery jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.stions about jump starters with air compressors, so be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

#7881. If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

Cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

On Oct. 23, NHTSA announced a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”

“As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”

Cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

Mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The company has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

“Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the company said in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

Those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

#7878. 13 Retailers You Never Knew Would Recycle Your Old Stuff

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 10, 2026 11:43 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As consumers, we create a massive amount of waste, filling up landfills with all of the products we’ve used and thrown away. While most people have a recycling bin along with their trash bin, they might not realize that many stores they frequent offer exceptional recycling programs for the items that can’t go in the recycling container.

These major retailers have robust recycling programs that can refurbish and reuse your old clothes, smartphones, rechargeable batteries, or furniture. And, for items that aren’t reusable, the retailers partner with recycling companies that can break them down into their base components to create a variety of other products.

“These sort of recycling programs are of huge importance,” says Paula Napolitano, product sales manager at Wisetek, a major Ireland-based distributor of refurbished and recycled electronics. “Last year there were around 59 million metric tons of e-waste generated globally, which is hugely impacting the environment. If large amounts of old electronics are allowed to build up in landfills, they can eventually begin to leach toxic materials into the soil, which may seriously harm the surrounding environment,” Napolitano says.

While lowering the impact you have on the local landfill is reason enough to hand off unwanted furniture, bedsheets, tablets, or rechargeable batteries to these retailers, you might be surprised to know that many of these companies offer additional incentives in the form of coupons, gift cards, and trade-in deals. Ahead, learn more about some of the top retailers who will take your unwanted stuff.

The big-box appliance and electronics giant is a leader in recycling, reusing, or repurposing, to the tune of 2.7 billion pounds of e-waste and appliances since 2009. You can drop off old electronics like computers, smartphones, radios, and more at any of Best Buy’s more than 1,000 locations and receive special promotions off certain products in the store. You can even earn gift cards for those items that still have value. Best Buy will also haul old TVs, fitness equipment, and appliances away for a nominal fee when you buy new ones.

“You can recycle up to three items per household per day,” says Alejandra Valeriano, public relations representative for Best Buy. “For $199.99, we’ll haul away and recycle up to a total of two large products (including TVs, major appliances, all-in-one computers and monitors), along with an unlimited number of select smaller products,” Valeriano says. Best Buy partners with Electronic Recyclers International, which breaks down electronics into materials that can be repurposed for use in everything from fiber optic cables to airplanes.

Few retailers have as robust a recycling program as The Home Depot. Consumers can access their comprehensive recycling web page that explains how to recycle everything from plastic plant pots to florescent tube lights. The company partners with nonprofit recycling company The Battery Network (formerly Call2Recycle) to recycle a variety of battery types, including those for power tools, EVs, and e-bikes. In 2024, The Home Depot recycled approximately 1 million pounds of rechargeable batteries. The retailer also collects plastic bags for composite manufacturer Trex, which uses them to make fencing and decking.

Not only will Staples recycle your old office supplies and electronics, they’ll pay you for it. Since 2012, Staples has recycled nearly 188 million pounds of technology. “Staples wants to make recycling easier for everyone across the U.S.,” says Mike Sauchuk, senior director of recycling and sustainability of Staples. “There are many items out there that we use every day that can be recycled, but it can be challenging to find a place to recycle them. That’s where Staples steps in. We offer free recycling for many hard-to-recycle items like technology, writing instruments, phone cases, and more. There’s no more waiting for your town’s local recycling day or event. At Staples, it’s recycling day every day.”

Through the Staples Rewards program, you can earn $5 back in rewards when you recycle tech and $2 back on every recycled ink or toner cartridge brought to one of the store’s more than 1,000 locations. In addition, the retailer will take unwanted electronics and worn-out rechargeable batteries for free.

Like other retailers, Walmart will take used cell phones, Bluetooth speakers, laptops, gaming consoles, tablets, and other devices through its trade-in program. Simply input info about the device on the Walmart website, get an offer for it, then ship it for free via FedEx or UPS Ground using a preprinted label. You receive an instant Walmart gift card for your efforts.

The presence of mercury, cadmium, lithium, and lead in car batteries ranks these vital components of cars and trucks among the more harmful products for the environment. Advance Auto Parts knows this, and therefore the company offers a nice incentive for bringing in your old battery once it dies. Take the worn-out battery to any Advance store and you’ll get a $10 gift card, which you can put toward the cost of a new battery or anything else in the store. The old batteries are then used to manufacture new ones.

While Apple’s products might be on the more expensive side when it comes to consumer electronics, they hold some of their value. That’s because the company makes it easy to cash in on that old iPhone, iPad, Macbook, or Apple Watch by allowing owners of the devices to trade their electronics in at an Apple Store or online. In return, Apple gives the customer store credit (Apple will also recycle other brands of electronics for free).

If the device is in good shape, it will be refurbished and resold. Those that can’t be reused go to one of Apple’s recycling partners, where they are broken down and recycled. Many iPhones end up with Daisy, Apple’s disassembly robot, which is designed to recover a device’s usable parts.

Habitat for Humanity’s ReStore has more than 900 locations nationwide, all of which will take appliances, furniture, various household items, and even building materials. Habitat then resells these items in its store and uses the proceeds to build affordable homes for families. “New and gently used items donated to a Habitat ReStore are resold to the community at a fraction of retail prices and help to support Habitat for Humanity’s vision of a world where everyone has a decent place to live,” says Jared Williams, communications manager at Habitat for Humanity International.

According to Williams, “Habitat ReStores tend to accept both new and gently used household items and building materials, which can include a wide variety of products.” He adds that donations come from all kinds of sources, “from neighbors completing home projects to restaurants after a remodel.” Habitat might not offer you a gift card for your stuff, but you can take tax deductions for your donations, since Habitat is a nonprofit organization.

RELATED: Don’t Throw Your Old Christmas Lights in the Trash—Do This Instead

Ever wonder where the used products Amazon sells come from? The online retailing behemoth accepts your old electronics and devices, including Bluetooth speakers and headphones, home security devices, wireless routers, and gaming systems. The company will even reward you with gift cards for gently used electronics that it can refurbish and resell. Amazon also takes some products that are no longer functioning. The company will recycle a variety of electronic devices for free, even covering the cost of shipping them to Amazon via UPS.

Bedding, unmatched socks, old T-shirts—clothing retailer H&M will take all linens as part of the company’s recycling program. Since 2013, H&M has collected more than 172,000 tons of textiles. The items were either cleaned and reused as second-hand clothing, turned into other products such as cleaning rags, or recycled into materials like insulation. When you drop off a bag of used clothing at H&M, the company will give you a coupon toward your next purchase at their store.

More than 1 billion HP ink and toner cartridges have been recycled by customers through the company’s HP Planet Partners program. The program aims to give a second life to HP’s end-of-life equipment and printing supplies and to reduce the environmental impact of electronic waste and greenhouse gas emissions. Simply drop off your HP ink and toner supplies at a location near you, mail them back, or request a pickup if you have a large quantity of supplies to give back.

Calling all coffee enthusiasts! If you own a Nespresso machine, you might be familiar with the company’s recycling program. Fill a Nespresso recycling bag (available for free at any Nespresso store) with your used capsules and drop them off at one of the 122,000-plus collection points around the world. The aluminum from the pods is recycled into items such as bicycles, computers, and soda cans, while the used coffee grounds create compost or green energy.

Kroger recognizes that most shoppers throw out plastic grocery bags and packaging after shopping, so they’ve put a special system in place for customers to take your discarded grocery bags and packaging and recycle them responsibly. The retail giant provides convenient drop-off bins to recycle plastic. The grocery chain has recycled more than 180 million pounds of plastic and aims to eliminate single-use plastic grocery bags in all of their stores by 2025.

Williams-Sonoma has a variety of initiatives dedicated to creating a more circular economy. The company works with donation programs like Good360 to give away returned and unsold products to local nonprofit organizations and others. They are also exploring rental and resale business models to give a second life to products like bedding, curtains, throws, pillows, linens, and more.

#7877. 5 Smart Tips for Soundproofing Windows

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Gretchen Heber, Bob Vila, Manasa Reddigari

Updated Nov 10, 2026 12:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Whether it’s highway traffic, loud neighbors, or birds chirping, if you don’t have sound proof windows, some noise from the outside world is bound to disrupt your daily activities, especially if the racket intrudes when you’re in a bedroom or other area intended as a sanctuary or work space. While you can’t control what goes on outside, you can block (or at least reduce) the noise by soundproofing windows using these techniques. Whether you implement one of these strategies or a combination thereof, you may find that soundproofing windows is your secret to attaining inner peace.

Soundproofing windows in your home can help you dampen noise for better sleep, and block out ambient noise in your home office. Window inserts are probably the most effective options, but they are expensive—they’ll set you back $300 to $800 per insert. Replacing older single-pane windows with updated double-pane windows, which cost $350 to $900 (and sometimes more) is another effective solution, albeit another big investment. A more affordable way to soundproof windows is to seal window gaps with acoustic caulk, which costs just $10 to $20. Sound-reducing window treatments, which start at about $20 each, are another cost-effective way to go.

If you live in an environment with heavy noise pollution, such as honking car horns, wailing sirens, or music blasting from next door, utilizing soundproofing window inserts is the most effective way to reduce the cacophony. These glass inserts are installed in the window frame a few inches in front of the interior face of your existing window. The air space between the insert and the window keeps most sound vibrations from passing through the glass, resulting in greater noise-reduction benefits than double-pane windows alone (more on these ahead). The most effective inserts are made of laminated glass, a thick glass consisting of two layers of glass with an intervening layer of plastic that effectively blocks vibrations. Some companies that make these inserts include Indow, Soundproof Windows, and CitiQuiet.

On the Sound Transmission Class (STC) scale that reflects the decibel reduction in noise volume that a window provides, soundproof windows typically measure between 48 and 54—the higher the STC, the greater the noise-reduction benefit. At the upper end, this means that a 98-decibel (db) outside noise (e.g., a motorcycle engine) is heard at only 44 db indoors (98 minus 54), which is no louder than a typical indoor conversation. You’ll get more noise reduction benefits by installing an insert in front of a single-pane window than you would with a double-pane window. This is because the STC of a double-pane window is often higher to begin with, so an insert won’t increase its overall STC as substantially. An insert for one window typically costs between $350 and $800 installed, which is less than or equal to the cost of the next option for soundproofing windows: a window replacement.

If you experience moderate outdoor noise pollution, such as the occasional lawn mower or a passing car, you may wish to replace single-pane windows with double-pane windows. Single-pane pane windows, often found in homes 15 years old or older, have just a single piece of glass in the window frame, while double-pane windows, the standard in newer homes, consist of two pieces of glass with air between them. Single-pane windows provide no air barrier between the outside and the glass, so they permit virtually all outdoor sounds to vibrate through the glass, resulting in a noisy interior.

Single-pane windows have an STC of between 26 and 28, which is only a little over half that of soundproof windows. At the upper end of this range, the window would reduce the noise volume of a passing car (70 db) to 42 db (70 minus 28). In contrast, the air space between the individual panes of a double-pane window helps halt the vibration of outdoor sounds through the glass, resulting in greater noise reduction benefit translating to an STC of 26 to 35. Compared with a single-pane window with an STC of 28, a double-pane window measuring in at 35 would reduce the noise volume of a passing car to only 35 db—offering a 7-decibel greater reduction in noise than the single-pane window (70 minus 35). While this may not seem like much, to the listener, a 7-db difference results in a perceived volume reduction of around 87 percent. Replacing one single-pane window with a double-pane equivalent will run you $350 to $900.

RELATED: Soundproofing a Room: The Two Best Ways to Dampen Noise Without Tearing Down Your Walls

Small gaps between a window frame and an interior wall can let outdoor noise into your home and keep your windows from performing at their STC rating. A simple way to seal these gaps is to fill them with an acoustic caulk, such as Green Glue Acoustical Caulk. This noiseproof, latex-based product reduces sound transmission and maintains windows’ STC but still allows you to open and close the windows.

Applying acoustic caulk is the easiest and most inexpensive way to soundproof windows. If there is already silicone caulk around the window frame, remove it with a putty knife. Cut a quarter-inch opening in the tip of the acoustic caulk tube with a utility knife, load the tube into a caulking gun, and pull the gun’s trigger to apply a thin bead of caulk in the gap between the interior window frame and interior wall.

Acoustic caulk readily bonds with most window frame and wall materials, including wood and drywall. More flexible than regular silicone caulk, acoustic caulk won’t shrink or form new cracks over time as you operate your windows; it’s also ultra-durable, lasting for several years before it requires re-caulking. Though you’ll most often find it white, acoustic caulk is available in a variety of hues. Some products turn clear as they dry, while others remain their original color but can be painted to match the color of interior walls.

To soften noise as well as reduce harsh glare, hang sound-dampening curtains. PONY DANCE’s blackout curtains, which were the top overall pick in our tested guide to the best soundproof curtains, are a top-quality option. Sound-dampening curtains, which usually cost $20 to $60 per panel, are made of a thick, heavy fabric such as velvet, and are typically lined with vinyl or a similar material that absorbs sound. These curtains also minimize echoes. Because they dampen but do not block sound entirely, they’re better suited for light noise pollution that may interrupt sleep, such as crickets or birds chirping, than they are for dampening the sound of heavy street traffic.

Many of these window treatments also serve as quality blackout curtains, which have a foam backing that helps block out light. Curtains that absorb sound and block light are great options for soundproofing bedrooms and other spaces designed for sleep and relaxation. They are especially popular with people who work night-shift hours and sleep during the day.

These lightweight linen blackout curtains reduced sound by 5 decibels in our hands-on testing. See our full review.

Cellular shades, also known as honeycomb shades, consist of rows of cells or hexagonal tubes of fabric stacked on top of each other. These shades serve several purposes: They block out light, prevent indoor heat gain in the summer and retain heat in winter, and absorb sound that vibrates into a room to reduce the echo. While single-cell shades have a single layer of cells and absorb limited sound, double-cell shades (such as those by First Rate Blinds) have two layers of cells and thus absorb more sound. Like sound-dampening curtains, they’re best suited for people who experience low levels of noise pollution.

Whether you live in an urban apartment where the noise of blaring horns is enough to drive you mad, or in a rural neighborhood where early-rising roosters create a cacophony, sometimes you just need relief from the racket. Addressing deficiencies in your windows’ soundproofing is one way to do that.

You may elect to replace your windows altogether, or you might choose to layer in some sound-blocking elements. Either way, relief from exterior racket isn’t too difficult to find. As for that drum kit your in-laws bought for the kids, you’re on your own there, though soundproofing your doors might be a good start.

The most affordable way to soundproof your windows is to caulk them with acoustic caulk. Remove any existing silicone caulk and recaulk with a product that is specifically designed to block window noise. A tube of acoustic caulk costs about $20. Window treatments are another economical way to soundproof your windows.

If you have single-pane windows or have no soundproofing materials in place, the sound of the wind blowing through the trees may be loud enough to permeate the windows. Or, you could be hearing wind whistling into the house, entering through gaps between window sashes and other parts of the window housing, such as the sill, jambs, or casing.

You can’t purchase 100 percent soundproof windows; they don’t exist. Noise-reduction windows can block up to 90 to 95 percent of sound.

#7876. The Best Holiday Decorations Across the U.S., and How to Steal the Look

These homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

Outdoor holiday decorating is an art. And while we love a tasteful string of white Christmas lights or a few pumpkins placed by the front door, why not really go for it when the holiday season rolls around? Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

From extra spooky Halloween displays to dazzling Christmas spectacles, these homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

A post shared by jessica archibald (@jessicarchibald)

Halloween 2026 has come and gone, but it’s never too early to start thinking about next year! Known simply as The Pumpkin House, @jessicarchibald lines her roof, porch, and yard with hundreds of jack-o’-lanterns every Halloween season. The piles of pumpkins make a big impact both during the day and at night.

Steal This Idea: All you need is pumpkins! Attach faux pumpkins to long boards to make them easier to display on the roof.

The Kraken House (@krakenhousenola) captured here by @amournola, uses blow-up decor to explore the haunted seas. The blow-up tentacles hint at a sea monster hiding beyond the windows, but the dramatic lighting is what really makes this house shine.

Steal This Idea: Skip the kid-friendly Bluey holiday inflatable this year, and attach these terrifying tentacles instead. Then turn up the drama with solar up-lights in green and purple.

Can you believe this amazing black cat is a DIY project? To transform this front porch into a Halloween stage, @allset_bygabrielle hand-carved the cat figure out of wood and painted every detail.

Steal This Idea: In addition to the vintage-inspired cat, the spooky forest framing the door was made with a mix of dead branches and faux botanicals; providing texture and a subtle sparkle.

This front entry in New York City (photographed by @victoria.nycvisit) uses dark drapery, black roses, and a wide variety of unique pumpkins and squashes to create a gothic masterpiece. Trick-or-treaters beware!

Steal This Idea: It’s amazing what a few swathes of black and burgundy fabric can do. Drape the fabric around your front door to make an eerie entrance. Then use pumpkins and vases full of dark flowers to complete the look.

This viral townhouse @stoopandthecity, is dressed to the nines for every holiday. This autumn harvest display features patterned pumpkins and cascades of fall foliage. It’s perfect for Thanksgiving or for those that prefer to skip the ghosts and goblins.

Steal This Idea: Choose faux and glass pumpkins in a cohesive color scheme, and don’t hold back on the fall foliage. Use faux stems to make the display last all season long.

A post shared by Marissa Fiala | Houston, TX (@houstonhotspots)

When it comes to Christmas lights, you can’t find much better than the extravagant homes in the River Oaks neighborhood of Houston, Texas. Each home goes all out with sparkling lights on its exterior, wrapped around every tree.

Steal This Idea: The secret to this colorful tree, captured by @houstonhotspots, is wrapping the lights tightly around the trunk and every single branch. The technique takes time but makes a big impact. Use LED lights to cut back on electricity use.

This famous house on Castro Street in San Francisco does not hold back! (Photo by @415urbanadventures.) Every exterior surface is covered in decor. The symmetrical layout keeps it looking classy instead of gaudy. And of course, the star of the show is Santa hanging in the middle, ready to deliver gifts.

Steal This Idea: The key element of this display is the garland covered in shiny Christmas ornaments. When you think you’ve gathered enough baubles, you’ll probably need even more!

The historic mill in Clifton, Ohio, is known for its over-the-top Christmas light display, featuring over four million lights! While you might not have a historic mill to decorate, the lighting techniques can be used on your own home to dazzle the entire neighborhood.

Steal This Idea: The most memorable element of this display is the iconic red lights cascading down the hillside. Try laying strings lights in rows along your entire yard to get a similar look.

A post shared by Joe Yost | Yost Team -Compass Pittsburgh (@joeyostteam)

Make your house look like one giant Christmas present by adding a larger-than-life red bow. This Pittsburgh mansion is famous for its red Christmas bow that looks beautifully whimsical in the daytime and lights up at night.

Steal This Idea: You don’t need a mansion to recreate this look. Get your own giant red bow and hang it above your front door. Here’s one available on Etsy!

A post shared by Pink Dreams Collection (@pinkdreamscollection)

One way to set your house apart for Christmas is to use a non-traditional color scheme —like pink! This darling cottage from @pinkdreamcollection is a frosted pink confection complete with pink trees and pink nutcracker figurines.

Steal This Idea: Pink or pastel Christmas decor will make your home look playful and unique. Use different shades of pink to add dimension.

A post shared by The Hazard’s Gingerbread House (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse)

This spectacular residential light display by Walter Hazard (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse) makes his home look like a technicolor gingerbread house. The secret is the wire-fencing frames he uses to create methodical light patterns. Visitors come from all over the area to witness the gorgeous lights in action.

Steal This Idea: We might not all have the same light-manipulation talent as Walter, but you can get the same grid-like coverage with LED curtain lights like these.

#7875. How to Use an Axe Safely

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 10, 2026 1:29 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Ever since someone put a club and stone together to make the first axe, it has remained a handy tool that has made life easier. Sure, you could fire up a chainsaw to do many things that an axe can do — like chopping wood for fuel, creating wood sculptures, prepping building materials, and clearing land, but an axe doesn’t require any fuel, is way easier to transport, and quieter.

While it may be one of the original tools that humans used, it’s still a tool that comes with risks and it’s important to know how to use an axe safely. It’s also crucial to know the differences among the various axes so you know which one will best suit your needs and how to use it safely and with the right technique.

It’s helpful to know the names for the main parts of an axe so that it’s easier to compare various models, and decide which type is right for your needs. Here are some key axe parts:

It’s not hard to imagine how things can go really wrong when using an axe. In addition to practicing with the axe so you feel confident using it, there are guidelines you should follow to stay safe.

While it may seem like power is the most important part of successful axe-swinging, control and technique have greater influence on success. Even though the weight of the axe helps increase the force, trying to swing an axe that’s too heavy for your abilities is never a good idea. You’ll have better success if you reach for an axe that’s a comfortable weight.

No matter the task, the technique for using an axe is similar.

Most felling strokes are diagonal, but some are horizontal to create a notch in the tree so it will fall. Always position your body (or halt your swing) so that the follow-through does not hit your body. And never stand in the path of where the tree may fall.

The Fiskars X27 is 36 inches long and weighs 6.3 pounds; requires strength to wield but cuts decisively. Read the review.

Limbing can be more dangerous than felling because you are dealing with smaller pieces and a great deal of sharp force near your body. Often, limbing happens while you are standing on a fallen tree. But if you aren’t, make sure there is ample distance between you and the arc of the axe swing. It’s usually easiest to start at the bottom of the tree and work your way to the top branches, swinging in the direction of the top of the tree as you go.

After a downed tree is limbed, it’s ready to be bucked into transportable lengths. Make sure the log won’t roll before you begin. Then, stand on the log and strike the axe below and between your feet.

Cutting logs along the grain is called splitting. A split log dries out faster, and will be ready quicker for a fireplace or fire pit. After placing a log vertically on a chopping block, aim at the face and swing the axe to make contact.

A competitive activity that’s become popular in recent years, axe throwing is usually done in a controlled space. While standing with your nondominant leg forward and at least 12 feet away from the target, pull the axe back over your head. With arms slightly bent, release the axe forward. Just like in golf, follow-through is essential.

Your axe will stay in great shape for a long time with proper care and maintenance. It only takes a few minutes after each use to keep it in fine shape. Plus, it will benefit from oiling and sharpening once a year.

Safely using an axe depends on careful planning about where and when you use the tool. It’s essential to select the right axe based on the task. And it takes practice to know how to hold an axe and how to swing an axe with ease. Never attempt to swing an axe if you feel nervous, if it’s dark out, or if people or pets are within your swing zone.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#7874. Plaintiffs Contesting Tren de Aragua Membership Claims / Alien Enemies Act Application Still Can't Sue Pseudonymously

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge James Wesley Hendrix (N.D. Tex.) Friday in W.M.M. v. Trump (for more on the earlier Fifth Circuit en banc decision, see here):

On March 14, 2025, the President invoked the Alien Enemies Act—a federal statute that permits the President to deport foreign nationals who are engaged in an "invasion or predatory incursion" against the United States—to detain and remove members of Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan terrorist group that traffics drugs and engages in other criminal activity. The petitioners, on behalf of a proposed class of Venezuelan nationals detained under the President's Proclamation, brought a habeas action in this Court. The petitioners argue that (1) the Proclamation exceeds the President's authority under the Alien Enemies Act and (2) the detainees have not received sufficient notice to challenge their removal.

After trips to the Fifth Circuit and the U.S. Supreme Court, the matter is back before this Court…. [T]he petitioners seek leave for the proposed class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms. The Court denies that motion because the named petitioners have not substantiated their conclusory allegations with evidence that they will suffer harm if their identities are disclosed. The Fifth Circuit found the petitioners' allegations insufficient to support their request to use pseudonyms [though it] {denied the petitioners' motion "without prejudice to any future determination by the district court regarding whether to allow any new class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms"}, and the petitioners have not persuaded this Court to depart from the Fifth Circuit's sound analysis….

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 10(a) "require[s] plaintiffs to disclose their names in the instrument they file to commence a lawsuit." "Public access to this information is more than a customary procedural formality; First Amendment guarantees are implicated when a court decides to restrict public scrutiny of judicial proceedings." … "Judicial records belong to the American people; they are public, not private, documents." … The Fifth Circuit thus recognizes a "strong presumption against party pseudonymity."

D.A.A., T.I.A., and E.A.A. "have not shown that disclosure of their names would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." … The petitioners do not request pseudonymity because the disclosure of their identities would reveal intimate details about their religion, sexuality, or family life. Rather, the petitioners do not want to disclose their identities because they do not want to publicize their alleged connection to TdA, a terrorist organization. But the Fifth Circuit has never suggested that this kind of information counts as a "sensitive and highly personal" matter that warrants pseudonymity.

Further, the petitioners dispute their designation as members of TdA. In other words, the petitioners allege that this designation is false. Yet the Fifth Circuit has implied that pseudonymity is proper only when the sensitive information—concerning, for example, one's religious beliefs—is true. Because the petitioners' alleged connection with TdA is, in their view, not true—and because it is not the kind of information that justifies pseudonymity—this Stegall factor cuts against the petitioners.

The Fifth Circuit also rejected the petitioners' argument that courts "should treat 'immigration matters, like the ones here, that disclose personal information,' as intimate information warranting pseudonymity," because the petitioners failed to explain how revealing "immigration matters" would "'disclose [any] personal information,' let alone information that makes pseudonyms appropriate." The petitioners have not provided any additional support for this argument to justify a departure from the Fifth Circuit's conclusion.

Relatedly, the Fifth Circuit rejected the petitioners' argument that they should be allowed to proceed under pseudonyms because several petitioners are seeking asylum. Two petitioners—T.I.A. and E.A.A.—seek asylum. The petitioners cite 8 C.F.R. § 208.6(a), which provides that information contained in an application for asylum "shall not be disclosed without the written consent of the applicant." But disclosing the petitioners' names will reveal only the fact that they have applied for asylum, not any information contained in the petitioners' respective asylum applications. {The information in the petitioners' respective asylum applications would likely not come before this Court anyway because the Court "lacks jurisdiction to hear an application for asylum."} Further, the petitioners still have not "shown that Venezuela penalizes asylum seekers." …

[P]etitioners [also] argue that public disclosure of their identities would subject them to physical violence in Venezuela. The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument because the petitioners expressed "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation, directed toward either them or their families, in Venezuela or other countries as a result of the U.S. government identifying them with TdA." In the Fifth Circuit's view, the petitioners failed to produce "'plausible predictions of possible future violence,' let alone evidence of 'express threats or incidents' to anyone, including them or their families, arising out of identification with TdA." The petitioners' "evidence-less, generalized fears" thus did not "overcome the presumption against pseudonymity."

The Fifth Circuit's sound conclusion follows from the principle that courts should "not usually allow parties to proceed anonymously based on generalized concerns." Indeed, the Fifth Circuit recognized that "[c]ourts generally allow pseudonymity if there is 'reasonable[]' 'fear[]' of 'retaliatory physical … harm to the requesting party or even more critically, to innocent non-parties,' which may be considered in light of 'the anonymous party's vulnerability to such retaliation.'" "Express threats of violence would likely qualify, as would specific past incidents of violence or vandalism." But the "[l]ack of such express threats or incidents—or at least lack of highly plausible predictions of possible future violence—will usually count against pseudonymity."

Seeking to surmount this hurdle, the petitioners have now provided "evidence not previously provided to the Fifth Circuit[] regarding risk of retaliation due to the government's designation" of the petitioners as members of TdA. In particular, the petitioners have provided an expert's declaration describing how TdA members face threats of physical violence from Venezuelan "paramilitary groups," "right-wing opposition leaders," and "[r]ival gangs." The expert's declaration also says that the Venezuelan government features TdA members—many of whom are detained at the Center for Terrorist Confinement (CECOT) in Tecoluca, El Salvador—in political propaganda and exposes them to political violence.

But this additional evidence still provides "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation." Each petitioner asserts that he "faces serious danger" of "retaliation, coercion, extortion, threatened prosecution, and violence from [TdA]-associated groups, rival gangs, and others" in El Salvador or Venezuela. But the petitioners have identified neither "express threats or incidents" nor "highly plausible predictions of possible future violence" to support pseudonymity. And the expert's declaration suffers from the same flaw. It says that alleged members of TdA "sometimes" face physical threats from groups that oppose the Venezuelan government, and "may" face threats or attacks from rival gangs. The two-page declaration lists no "[e]xpress threats of violence" or "specific past incidents of violence or vandalism" to support its generalized assertions.

Further, while the expert's declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime may use members of TdA detained at CECOT as "propaganda tools" and subject those detainees to "political violence," these suggestions are conclusory. The expert's declaration does not even connect (1) the potential disclosure of the petitioners' identities in this lawsuit with (2) the likelihood that the petitioners will be used as "propaganda tools" and accordingly face "political violence" in El Salvador or Venezuela. The declaration merely states that its conclusions are based on "the situation in Venezuela for the men sent by the United States to CECOT in March 2025." In this respect, the declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime singled out these men—and "disclos[ed] personal details about them"—solely on account of their detention at CECOT. Whether the detainees' identities were disclosed in a lawsuit in the United States was of no matter.

In any event, the Court lacks sufficient evidence to support the inference that denying the petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms will cause them to face threats or physical harm in the future. Thus, the petitioners have not persuaded this Court that its analysis of this issue should differ from the Fifth Circuit's, given the generalized, conclusory nature of the petitioners' allegations.

{The Court previously granted the original named petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms, because of "the sensitive and personal information about their immigration status and histories in this case." But the Court did so in a summary order at the inception of this litigation on a rapid timeline. Considering the en banc Fifth Circuit's statement on this matter and the lack of compelling evidence to distinguish the petitioners' present arguments from the arguments that the Fifth Circuit found unpersuasive, the Court finds it appropriate to deny the petitioners' motion for leave to proceed under pseudonyms.}

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 9, 1942

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7872. That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

Those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

The hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

Hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

#7870. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

Tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

Both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

They give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, issue an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

“Each office knows the local area and will issue Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”

Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

“Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Warnings, Watches and Advisories” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Resources and Frequently Asked Questions” National Weather Service, “Prepare! Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”

#7867. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

By Jenn Ryan, Katie Barton, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor

Hydroponic systems, which allow plants to grow in water rather than soil, are popular because they offer a way to produce a bounty of plants in a relatively small area in an indoor garden. These systems also tend to be user-friendly, so even newbie growers are likely to succeed. We recently tested eight popular models, spending several months setting them up and evaluating their various features while growing a range of plants.

We also evaluated each tested hydroponics system for its ease of use, value, functionality, appearance, and build quality. With these factors in mind, our favorite is Ahopegarden’s 10-Pod Aeroponics Growing Kit. It offers the flexibility to grow almost any type of plant, is easy to set up, and provides a good value for the money.

But Ahopegarden isn’t the only show in town. Some of the other kits we tested also ranked highly and may better fit your indoor gardening needs depending on the available space and desired setup. Check out our top picks of some of the best hydroponic systems to get started.

Bottom line: Explore the best hydroponic systems of 2026, from compact kits to large setups, each offering unique features for indoor gardening success.

To qualify as one of our top picks, we required each hydroponic system to have a water circulation system to keep the water fresh. When evaluating all-inclusive systems, we looked for bright grow lights that could be adjusted in height as the plants grow taller. The following hydroponic systems vary in design and size, but each is well suited to growing healthy herbs and plants indoors.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

The Ahopegarden offers an affordable way to grow fruits, vegetables, or flowers at home. It has the capacity to grow 10 plants and comes with baskets, sponges, plant food, and grow domes—everything needed to get started except for seeds. While this system can be used to produce any type of plant, the adjustable light reaches a maximum height of 14.6 inches, so users will need to select plant varieties that won’t exceed this.

We chose a dwarf tomato variety and mini bell pepper to grow in our Ahopegarden, planting five of each seed. Setting the system up required us to soak the sponges, fill the water tank, and use tweezers to add 2 to 3 seeds to each sponge (some larger seeds must be soaked for 6 to 12 hours before planting). We added grow domes to our plant pods and selected the “vegetable” button on the top of the light panel, which put the grow light on the appropriate timer.

We love this system’s flexibility. It’s also on the smaller side, so it’s easy to find a spot for it, even in cramped spaces. Our biggest concern is that there isn’t much spacing between the pods, so depending on the plant, it can get crowded.

What our tester says: “The Ahopegarden was simple to set up. We love that it has automatic lights for growing fruits and flowers or vegetables. We planted dwarf tomatoes and mini bell peppers in our growing kit, and they sprouted within a week.”—Katie Barton, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Ahopegarden hydroponic system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 4/5

The AeroGarden Bounty grows up to nine plants and comes with a seed kit of the user’s choice. Thanks to a convenient touch screen, growers can easily set their own light and watering schedule, and there’s a vacation mode for when the system will be unattended.

One of the system’s best features is its tall grow height of 24 inches—the highest of any smaller hydroponic system in our lineup. The grow height makes it easier to nurture larger plant varieties, such as peppers and tomatoes, without worrying about plants getting their leaves singed on the lights. The system also includes a trellis, which is helpful when growing such larger plants.

The Bounty has a large water reservoir, so the system needs minimal topping off. It also comes with liquid plant food and humidity caps for seeds to germinate. However, in testing—growing a combination of lettuces and herbs—the width of the system proved a bit short. This led to stunted growth of some plants, while others competed for light. For example, when we placed cilantro and a short lettuce variety next to each other, the cilantro grew taller and blocked light from the lettuce, which failed to truly thrive.

While AeroGarden could fix this problem by making the Bounty wider, we found the solution to be simply using fewer grow stations simultaneously. When replanting seeds in the system during a second round of testing, we planted fewer plants (six instead of nine) and found that they did better, growing larger and looking healthier.

What our tester says: “Despite the width of the system being a bit short for my preferences, after I figured out how to work around this issue, the AeroGarden Bounty earned one of the best overall spots for the number of plants it grows, its reasonable price, its tall grow height, and for being an inclusive kit that makes hydroponics simple.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the AeroGarden Bounty hydroponic system at Amazon or AeroGarden.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 5/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

Few gardening processes are more straightforward than taking cuttings from existing houseplants or vines and starting them in water. The TomGear hydroponic garden includes three see-through glass bulbs to fill with water to encourage root development. Its wood framing also serves as an attractive decoration for a sunny windowsill or countertop.

While the system doesn’t include LED lights or a water-recirculating pump, it works via a tried-and-true plant-propagation method that is simple but effective. When roots develop, plants can be transplanted into pots or to an outdoor garden spot.

During testing, we found this system was very easy to set up. We also appreciated its small size and good looks; it could beautify just about any spot that gets enough natural light for plants. However, we found the necks of the glass vases to be quite narrow—while we could easily fit herbs (such as the rosemary we rooted), we had trouble getting snake plants and succulents into the water. When we received the Plantaform grow kit, we were impressed by its quality, futuristic look. The instructions for setting it up weren’t quite as clear as those for other growing systems we tried. However, once we figured out what to do, it only took about fifteen minutes to get everything set up.

Our lettuce seeds sprouted within a few days, and we were able to remove the germination domes. We then relied on the app to inform us when to add water and nutrients and harvest the plants. Unfortunately, the app malfunctioned a few times, telling us to harvest at one week and then again at two weeks when the plants were still tiny.
